claims.text: The claim that both goods and services consumer spending rose in Q1 2024 is false: services spending rose but goods spending fell, according to the BEA second estimate.

citations.quotation: The increase in consumer spending reflected an increase in services that was partly offset by a decrease in goods. Within services, the leading contributors to the increase were health care as well as financial services and insurance. Within goods, the leading contributors to the decrease were motor vehicles and parts as well as gasoline and other energy goods.

claims.text: Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 1.3 percent in the first quarter of 2024, per the BEA second estimate, revised down 0.3 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily due to a downward revision to consumer spending.

citations.quotation: Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 1.3 percent in the first quarter of 2024, according to the “second” estimate. In the fourth quarter of 2023, real GDP increased 3.4 percent. The GDP estimate for the first quarter was revised down 0.3 percentage point from the “advance” estimate, primarily reflecting a downward revision to consumer spending.

counterarguments.text: Consumer spending overall did increase in Q1 2024, so a weaker version of the claim (that consumer spending rose) is supported; only the goods-and-services-specific version is contradicted.

citations.quotation: The increase in the first quarter primarily reflected increases in consumer spending and housing investment that were partly offset by a decrease in inventory investment.

limitations: The GDP aggregate figure (1.3 percent) alone cannot establish the composition of consumer spending; it does not show the split between goods and services, which the source provides only in a separate passage.
Excerpts are partial; the sources note the third estimate (due June 27, 2024) may further revise figures.
Declared publication date (2024-05-30) is not independently verified.
No contrary passage claims goods spending rose; the goods decline is directly stated, so there is no cited opposing evidence for the original claim.
